title: Maximum Sum of 3 Non-Overlapping Subarrays
description: Brute force to optimized: resumming every triple of window positions versus fixing the middle window and precomputing the best left/right neighbors.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find three non-overlapping subarrays, each of length exactly k, that together maximize the sum of their elements. Return the starting indices of the three subarrays, in increasing order; if multiple answers tie for the maximum sum, return the lexicographically smallest set of indices.

blocks.caption: Precompute the best window to the left and to the right of every position, then try every possible middle window

blocks.text: Given nums and k, choose 3 non-overlapping subarrays of length k each, maximizing their combined sum, returning the lexicographically smallest set of starting indices if there's a tie.

blocks.title: Analogy: Picking the Best 3 Non-Overlapping Ad Slots on a Timeline
blocks.text: Like scheduling 3 non-overlapping advertising slots of a fixed duration along a timeline of varying viewership numbers, wanting the 3 slots that together capture the most total viewers. Rather than checking every possible combination of 3 slot positions, precomputing "the best single slot to the left of here" and "the best single slot to the right of here" for every position lets every possible middle slot be paired instantly with its best possible neighbors.

blocks.text: Before checking every possible triple of window positions directly, notice that fixing the MIDDLE window's position turns the remaining choice into two completely independent, simpler sub-problems.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every length-k window's sum can be precomputed once with a standard fixed-size sliding window, in O(n) total.

Observation 2: If the middle window's position is fixed, the best possible left window is simply the highest-sum window entirely before it, and the best possible right window is simply the highest-sum window entirely after it -- these two choices don't affect each other at all once the middle is fixed.

Observation 3: Precompute left[i] (the index of the best window anywhere in [0, i]) and right[i] (the index of the best window anywhere in [i, end]) once, in O(n) total, using two more linear passes.

Observation 4: For every possible middle window position j (ranging only over positions that leave room for both a left and a right window), look up left[j-k] and right[j+k] in O(1), combine their sums with windowSums[j], and track the overall best combination.

Recognizing that fixing the middle window decouples the left and right choices completely is the key insight that turns an apparently cubic search into three linear passes.

This is a "fix the middle, precompute the best neighbors independently" technique, building on the fixed-size sliding window sum precomputation seen throughout this category, plus two auxiliary best-so-far arrays (one scanning left to right, one right to left).
For every possible triple of non-overlapping starting positions, sum all three windows directly and track the best combination.

items: For every possible starting index i of the first window, every possible starting index j of the second window (at least k positions after i), and every possible starting index l of the third window (at least k positions after j), sum all three windows directly.
Track the combination with the highest total sum, preferring the lexicographically smallest indices on a tie by only updating on a STRICTLY greater sum.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The three nested loops enforce non-overlap directly, since each subsequent starting index must be at least k positions after the previous window began.
Each window's sum is recomputed directly from nums for every triple, since this brute force does not yet share any precomputed sums.
Using a strict > comparison (not >=) when updating bestSum naturally keeps the first (lexicographically smallest, since indices are tried in increasing order) combination found among ties.

blocks.text: Every possible triple of non-overlapping window positions is checked directly, so the correct maximum combination is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed * k) in the worst case, from the three nested position loops combined with summing each window directly.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: resumming every window from scratch for every triple, and recombining every possible left/middle/right choice together, ignores that the best left and right window for ANY fixed middle position can each be precomputed once and reused.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force recomputes everything for every triple of positions. Instead, precompute windowSums once with a fixed-size sliding window. Then precompute left[i] (best window index in [0,i]) with one linear pass, and right[i] (best window index in [i,end]) with another. Finally, iterate over every possible middle window position j, looking up left[j-k] and right[j+k] in O(1) each, to find the best overall combination in a single additional linear pass.

Build windowSums with a fixed-size sliding window. Build left[] scanning left to right, tracking the best (strictly greatest, earliest-on-tie) window index seen so far. Build right[] scanning right to left, tracking the best (using >= to prefer the earliest index on a tie) window index seen so far. Then scan every valid middle position j, combining windowSums[left[j-k]], windowSums[j], and windowSums[right[j+k]], tracking the best combination.
Precompute window sums, then best-left and best-right arrays, then scan every possible middle window position.

codes.python:
def max_sum_of_three_subarrays(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    num_windows = n - k + 1
    window_sums = [0] * num_windows                                        # windowSums[i] = sum of nums[i:i+k], built with a fixed-size sliding window
    total = sum(nums[:k])
    window_sums[0] = total
    for i in range(k, n):
        total += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        window_sums[i - k + 1] = total

    left = [0] * num_windows                                                # left[i] = index of the best (earliest-on-tie) window in [0, i]
    best_left = 0
    for i in range(num_windows):
        if window_sums[i] > window_sums[best_left]:
            best_left = i
        left[i] = best_left

    right = [0] * num_windows                                               # right[i] = index of the best (earliest-on-tie) window in [i, end]
    best_right = num_windows - 1
    for i in range(num_windows - 1, -1, -1):
        if window_sums[i] >= window_sums[best_right]:                      # >= keeps the EARLIEST index among ties, for lexicographically smallest results
            best_right = i
        right[i] = best_right

    best_sum = -1
    result = []
    for j in range(k, num_windows - k):                                   # try every possible position for the MIDDLE window
        l, r = left[j - k], right[j + k]
        total = window_sums[l] + window_sums[j] + window_sums[r]
        if total > best_sum:
            best_sum = total
            result = [l, j, r]
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_sum_of_three_subarrays([1, 2, 1, 2, 6, 7, 5, 1], 2))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), across the four linear passes (window sums, left array, right array, middle scan) combined.
Space: O(n) for the three auxiliary arrays.

Once the middle window's position is fixed, the choice of left window (anywhere before it) and right window (anywhere after it) are completely independent of each other, so each can be optimized separately and combined. left[i] and right[i] precompute exactly these independent optimal choices for every possible position, letting every middle position be evaluated in O(1) using simple array lookups rather than a fresh scan.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Building left[] (left to right, strict >)","Keeps the EARLIEST index among ties, since ties are only replaced by a strictly greater sum"],["Building right[] (right to left, using >=)","Also keeps the EARLIEST index among ties, since scanning right-to-left with >= lets an equally-good, more-leftward index overwrite a later one"]]}

items: windowSums is built with the standard fixed-size sliding window technique seen throughout this category (add the entering element, subtract the leaving one).
left[] uses a strict > when updating bestLeft, naturally preferring the earliest index when sums tie (since a later equal sum won't override an earlier one).
right[] uses >= (not >) specifically so that, scanning from the right, an equally good but more-leftward window correctly overwrites bestRight, ensuring the leftmost tie is kept there too.

blocks.text: Fixing the middle element of a 3-way combination and precomputing the best choice independently on each side is a broadly reusable technique whenever a problem asks for an optimal combination of several non-overlapping, mutually independent pieces.

items: Using > instead of >= when building the right[] array, which would incorrectly keep a LATER index on a tie instead of the required lexicographically smallest (earliest) one.
Forgetting to bound the middle window's position (j must leave room for both a valid left window and a valid right window), leading to out-of-bounds lookups.
Recomputing window sums with a fresh O(k) summation at each position instead of using the fixed-size sliding window's O(1) incremental update.

items: Explicitly explain the "fix the middle, the left and right choices become independent" insight before coding, since it's the key structural realization that makes this problem tractable in linear time.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find k non-overlapping fixed-length windows maximizing a combined property" (especially for small, fixed k like 2 or 3) points toward fixing one window's position and precomputing the best choices for the others independently, using auxiliary best-so-far arrays.

items: How would this generalize to finding 4 or more non-overlapping windows? The "fix one, precompute the rest" technique becomes harder to apply directly with more pieces; a more general DP over "best combined sum using the first i windows, having placed j of the k required subarrays" would be needed instead.

What if the subarrays could have variable (not fixed) length? This changes the problem substantially, since a fixed-size sliding window can no longer precompute all relevant sums in a simple array; a different DP formulation would be required.

How would you verify the lexicographic tie-breaking is correct in all cases? Construct a test case with multiple genuinely tied maximum-sum combinations and confirm the leftmost one is returned, paying particular attention to the >= in the right[] construction.

Builds on the fixed-size sliding window sum precomputation used throughout Kadane's Algorithm and Sliding Window problems, combined with a "fix one piece, precompute the optimal choice for the others independently" technique reusable in other fixed-k combination problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n cubed * k) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (fix the middle, precompute left/right): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window sums, combined with precomputed best-window-to-the-left and best-window-to-the-right arrays
Core Idea: Fixing the middle window's position makes the best left and right window choices completely independent, letting every middle position be evaluated in O(1)
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Once the middle window is fixed, the optimal left and right windows can be looked up independently via precomputed best-so-far arrays
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Precompute windowSums, left[] (best before i), right[] (best from i onward); scan every middle position
